doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Sociology versus musicology in teaching jazz history
summary: Schoenberg says jazz development is sociology; his course starts with colonial New Orleans, and he credits Albert Murray and Stanley Crouch.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: You mentioned minstrel-y, you know, the minstrel practice.
Right. Still very prevalent in 2019. It is.
This is a hard — maybe a hard or way too simplistic question. But you teach jazz history, do you think that the development of the music has more to do with sociology or to do with musicology?

Because I mean, I’m a college dropout so let’s get that straight. So I don’t know a lot of terms to be conversant with necessarily, and I might be confusing some that someone with an academic background might hear me talking and right now they’re rolling their eyes. But what I mean is that — well you mentioned teaching jazz history. We don’t get to Jelly Roll Morton or Sidney Bechet for a couple of months. So you know it’s all about New Orleans and English and French mercantilism, and what it was like to be colonized by the French or by the English or by the Spanish, and about of course New Orleans and about the great lives of the nineteenth century and about Gottschalk, Louis Moreau Gottschalk, and about Abe Lincoln and, all these things, and without laying a strong predicate or whatever the right word would be for that, then I don’t think you can really start to understand, I should say not you of course but a young student of 2019 who may not be enmeshed in history like earlier generations were, that it’s necessary to create this context. And then maybe we can start to understand who Armstrong was and who Bechet was and who Benny Goodman was and all these things. So about minstrelsy, I learned a © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

lot from reading Albert Murray and then getting to know him and Stanley Crouch and others, and just doing a lot of reading and talking to people, including musicians of the much older generations. I mean I got to know Zutty Singleton’s wife pretty well, which I’ll talk about when we talk about the New York Jazz Museum, and trying to put it all together in some way that makes sense. So I don’t know if that answered your question.
